Memory.value: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette:
Rangi, a 75-year-old financial analyst with Oceania heritage, had lived most of their life with a steady, quiet confidence—managing portfolios, advising clients, raising a family alongside their late spouse. But the rape, which happened three years ago, shattered that. The details were never fully accessible. When Rangi tried to recall what exactly happened that evening after a client dinner, the story wouldn’t form. Instead, fragments surfaced: the metallic taste of blood from a bitten lip; the sound of the perpetrator’s belt buckle clinking, a sound that now appeared without warning in their head, crisp as the original moment, day or night. They could taste the blood again, feel the salt, smell the faint cologne. But the sequence of how they had gotten from the restaurant to that hotel room, or how they had left—those pieces were gone, a black gap in the timeline. What remained was a conviction: people could not be trusted to behave decently. The perpetrator had worn a suit, had smiled, had been a colleague’s associate. In Rangi’s mind, the event proved that beneath any polished surface, people were capable of profound moral violation.

Weeks after, Rangi noticed a creeping dread in places that had never bothered them before. The sight of a police cruiser idling at an intersection made their chest tighten and their palms sweat. Once, nearing a precinct to file a routine financial report, they turned around and walked ten blocks the other way. They did not know why police felt dangerous—they had never interacted with them that night—but the uniform, the authority, the possibility of being questioned or not believed felt like a direct threat. At work, a supervisor’s gentle correction on a spreadsheet model sent a spike of heat through Rangi’s body. Being criticized now meant something more than a professional remark; it felt like an accusation, a sign that their own judgment was fundamentally flawed. Rangi began to avoid meetings where their work might be reviewed. They stopped speaking up during team discussions. They started arriving early to slip their reports under office doors rather than hand them to colleagues. The isolation grew, but it felt safer.

The meaning that had once animated Rangi’s life—the satisfaction of a well-calculated risk, the pride in mentoring junior analysts, the quiet joy of gardening after a long week—had drained away. Nothing felt meaningful. Not the portfolio they had managed for thirty years, not the house now filled only with their collection of seashells and photographs of a spouse who had died a decade before the assault. Rangi had, for years, been the steady one. Now they could not rely on themselves. They would second-guess a grocery list, replay a conversation obsessively, worry that they had missed some crucial sign of danger. The reactions themselves—the sudden taste of blood in the checkout line, the sound of a belt buckle during a quiet evening—frightened Rangi most of all. They began to believe that their mind was breaking apart, that they were going crazy. No one else they knew lived like this. No one else tasted trauma, heard it, felt it without warning, and could not even tell the story of how it began.

By the time Rangi sought help, they had stopped going to the office altogether. Their supervisor had called three times, concerned. Rangi’s eldest child had noticed the withdrawal, the sharp silence during phone calls. What brought them to the clinic was not hope, exactly, but a weary acknowledgment that living this way—fragmented, afraid of criticism, mistrusting every stranger and every authority, and carrying an unspoken taste in the mouth—was not living. Rangi sat in the waiting room with their hands folded, wondering whether a therapist would correct them, or fail to believe them, or somehow confirm that they were, in fact, losing their mind. What they most wanted, beneath the fear, was to find even one piece of a coherent story that they could hold onto without flinching.
